37977.e: A superpower has a large military, lots of money and great influence all over the world. In the Cold War there were two of them.
37977.m: In the Cold War, the USA and the Soviet Union were two superpowers.

37978.q: Which city is the capital of the USA?
37978.e: The President, Congress and the Supreme Court of the USA work in Washington. New York is bigger, but it is not the capital.
37978.m: Washington is the capital of the USA.

37979.q: In which building does the President of the USA live and work?
37979.e: The White House in Washington is the official residence of the President of the USA. It is called that because of its white colour.
37979.m: The President of the USA lives and works in the White House.

37980.q: During the Cold War, which was the largest country on Earth by area?
37980.e: The Soviet Union stretched from Europe to the Pacific. It was bigger than any other country.
37980.m: The Soviet Union was the largest country on Earth.

37981.q: Which language was the most important in the Soviet Union?
37981.e: Many peoples with their own languages lived in the Soviet Union. But Russian was the shared language that everyone learned at school.
37981.m: Russian was the most important language in the Soviet Union.

37982.q: What is the flag of the USA called because of the way it looks?
37982.e: The flag of the USA has 13 red and white stripes and 50 white stars on a blue background. That is why it is called the ‘Stars and Stripes’.
37982.m: The flag of the USA is called the Stars and Stripes.

37983.q: What is the money of the USA called?
37983.e: In the USA people pay with the US dollar. It is one of the most important currencies in the world.
37983.m: The money of the USA is called the dollar.

37984.q: Which of the two superpowers was governed by communists?
37984.e: In the Soviet Union only the Communist Party governed. The USA was a democracy with several parties.
37984.m: The Soviet Union was the communist superpower.

37985.q: Which British politician made the expression ‘Iron Curtain’ famous in 1946?
37985.e: In a speech in the USA in 1946, Winston Churchill said that an iron curtain divided Europe. After that the expression became known all over the world.
37985.m: Winston Churchill made the expression ‘Iron Curtain’ famous.

37986.q: Which continent did the Iron Curtain divide?
37986.e: The Iron Curtain ran from north to south right across Europe. It separated Western Europe from Eastern Europe.

37987.q: According to Churchill, on which sea did the Iron Curtain begin in the north?
37987.e: Churchill said the curtain stretched from Stettin on the Baltic to Trieste. Stettin, now called Szczecin, is in Poland today.
37987.m: In the north, the Iron Curtain began on the Baltic Sea.

37988.q: According to Churchill, on which sea did the Iron Curtain end in the south?
37988.e: Churchill named the port city of Trieste on the Adriatic as the southern end. The Adriatic is part of the Mediterranean.
37988.m: In the south, the Iron Curtain ended on the Adriatic.

37989.q: Which country was the first to start taking down its border fence with the West in 1989?
37989.e: In May 1989 Hungary began to take down the fence on its border with Austria. Soon many people from East Germany fled to the West via Hungary.
37989.m: In 1989 Hungary was the first country to open a hole in the Iron Curtain.

37990.q: Which of Switzerland’s neighbours bordered directly on the Iron Curtain?
37990.e: Austria bordered on Czechoslovakia and Hungary, which both belonged to the Eastern Bloc. Austria itself was neutral.
37990.m: Austria lay right on the Iron Curtain.

37991.q: What was the Iron Curtain mainly meant to prevent?
37991.e: The governments in the East did not want their citizens to flee to the West. That is why the border was strictly guarded.
37991.m: The Iron Curtain was meant to prevent escape to the West.

37992.q: What is the strip of nature that runs along the former Iron Curtain today called?
37992.e: In the former border strip, plants and animals were able to spread undisturbed for decades. Today it is protected as the Green Belt.
37992.m: Where the Iron Curtain once stood, there is now the Green Belt.

37993.q: In which year was NATO founded?
37993.e: NATO was founded on 4 April 1949. It was meant to protect the Western countries together.

37994.q: What kind of organisation is NATO?
37994.e: In NATO, countries have joined together to defend each other. That is why it is called a military alliance.

37995.q: In which city does NATO have its headquarters?
37995.e: NATO’s headquarters is in Brussels, the capital of Belgium.
37995.m: NATO has its headquarters in Brussels.

37996.q: How many member countries does NATO have (as of 2026)?
37996.e: Many countries have joined since it was founded. In 2026 NATO has 32 members.

37997.q: What is the most important principle of NATO?
a: An attack on one counts as an attack on all
Every country has its own army
37997.e: If one member is attacked, this counts as an attack on all members. Then the countries help each other.
37997.m: In NATO, an attack on one member counts as an attack on all.

37998.q: Which symbol can be seen on the NATO flag?
37998.e: The flag is dark blue with a white compass rose, like on a compass. It stands for the members’ shared path.
37998.m: There is a compass rose on the NATO flag.

37999.e: Sweden was neutral for a long time and joined NATO in March 2024. Finland had already joined a year earlier.
37999.m: Sweden has been a member of NATO since 2024.

38000.q: Which ocean is NATO named after?
38000.e: NATO stands for ‘North Atlantic Treaty Organization’. Its members lie on both sides of the Atlantic.
38000.m: NATO is named after the Atlantic.

38001.q: In which year was the Warsaw Pact founded?
38001.e: The Warsaw Pact was founded in May 1955. Shortly before that, West Germany had joined NATO.
38001.m: The Warsaw Pact was founded in 1955.

38002.q: In which country is the city that the Warsaw Pact is named after?
38002.e: The treaty was signed in Warsaw. Warsaw is the capital of Poland.
38002.m: The Warsaw Pact is named after the Polish capital, Warsaw.

38003.q: Which of these countries was a member of the Warsaw Pact?
38003.e: East Germany belonged to the Warsaw Pact from the start. Austria and Finland were neutral, and Yugoslavia went its own way.
38003.m: East Germany belonged to the Warsaw Pact.

38004.q: How many countries belonged to the Warsaw Pact at the start?
38004.e: At the start they were the Soviet Union, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, Albania and East Germany. That makes 8 countries.
38004.m: At the start, 8 countries belonged to the Warsaw Pact.

38005.q: Which country led the Warsaw Pact?
38005.e: The Soviet Union was the strongest power in the Warsaw Pact and decided what the alliance did. The treaty was signed in Warsaw, but it was led from Moscow.
38005.m: The Soviet Union led the Warsaw Pact.

38006.q: Which Western alliance was the opponent of the Warsaw Pact?
38006.e: The Warsaw Pact was the military alliance of the East. Facing it was the alliance of the West.
38006.m: The opponent of the Warsaw Pact was NATO.

38007.q: In which year was the Warsaw Pact dissolved?
38007.e: After the end of the communist governments in Eastern Europe, the alliance was no longer needed. It was dissolved in July 1991.

38008.e: The ball had a diameter of 58 centimetres. That is about as big as a large beach ball.
38008.m: Sputnik 1 was about as big as a large beach ball.

38009.q: In which year did Yuri Gagarin fly into space?
38009.e: Gagarin took off on 12 April 1961. Today this day is celebrated as the International Day of Human Space Flight.
38009.m: Yuri Gagarin flew into space in 1961.

38010.q: Which country did Yuri Gagarin come from?
38010.e: Gagarin was a pilot in the Soviet Air Force. He came from a small village in Russia.
38010.m: Yuri Gagarin came from the Soviet Union.

38011.q: How many times did Yuri Gagarin orbit the Earth?
38011.e: Gagarin flew around the Earth exactly once. Then he landed back in the Soviet Union.
38011.m: Yuri Gagarin orbited the Earth once.

38012.q: Roughly how long did Yuri Gagarin’s flight last?
38012.e: From take-off to landing, the flight lasted about 108 minutes. That is just under two hours.
38012.m: Yuri Gagarin’s flight lasted just under two hours.

38013.q: What are space travellers from the Soviet Union and Russia called?
38013.e: In Russia they say cosmonaut, in the USA astronaut. Space travellers from China are called taikonauts.
38013.m: Space travellers from Russia are called cosmonauts.

38014.q: What did Yuri Gagarin shout in Russian at take-off?
38014.e: At take-off Gagarin shouted ‘Poyekhali!’. In English this means ‘Let’s go!’ and is very well known in Russia today.
38014.m: At take-off, Yuri Gagarin shouted ‘Let’s go!’.

38015.q: How old was Yuri Gagarin when he flew into space?
38015.e: Gagarin was born in 1934 and flew into space in 1961. So he was 27 years old.
38015.m: Yuri Gagarin was 27 years old on his space flight.

38016.q: Who was the second person to walk on the Moon?
38016.e: Buzz Aldrin followed the commander onto the Moon’s surface shortly afterwards. The two stayed outside for about two and a half hours.
38016.m: Buzz Aldrin was the second person on the Moon.

38017.q: Which Apollo 11 astronaut stayed in the spacecraft and orbited the Moon?
38017.e: Michael Collins waited in the command module ‘Columbia’ while the other two were on the Moon. He never walked on the Moon.
38017.m: Michael Collins orbited the Moon alone and waited for the others.

38018.q: How does the famous sentence continue: ‘That’s one small step for man, one ... for mankind’?
38018.e: The first person on the Moon said this sentence as he stepped onto the Moon’s surface. It is one of the best-known sentences in history.
38018.m: The first step on the Moon was a giant leap for mankind.

38019.q: Which Swiss university had an experiment on the Moon during Apollo 11?
38019.e: Researchers from Bern built a sail of aluminium foil that caught particles from the Sun. On the Moon it was even set up before the US flag.
38019.m: A solar wind experiment from the University of Bern was part of the first Moon landing.

38020.e: The Saturn V was over 100 metres tall and one of the most powerful rockets ever built. It sent the astronauts on their way to the Moon.
38020.m: Apollo 11 was launched on the huge Saturn V rocket.

a: Both sides build more and more weapons
38021.e: In the Cold War, the USA and the Soviet Union each wanted to be stronger than the other. So both sides built more and more, and ever stronger, weapons.
38021.m: In an arms race, opponents compete to build more and more weapons.

38022.q: Which especially dangerous weapons did the USA and the Soviet Union build in the arms race?
38022.e: Atomic bombs can destroy whole cities. Both superpowers built a great many of them.
38022.m: In the arms race, both sides built many atomic bombs.

38023.q: Which country was the first to have an atomic bomb?
38023.e: The USA tested the first atomic bomb in 1945. In the same year it used atomic bombs against Japan.
38023.m: The USA was the first country to have an atomic bomb.

38024.q: In which year did the Soviet Union test its first atomic bomb?
38024.e: In August 1949 the Soviet Union set off its first atomic bomb. Now both superpowers had this weapon.
38024.m: The Soviet Union had an atomic bomb from 1949.

38025.q: What do you call it when countries agree to reduce their weapons?
38025.e: In disarmament, weapons are destroyed or no longer built. It is the opposite of arming.
38025.m: Disarmament means countries have fewer weapons.

38026.q: Why did neither superpower use its atomic bombs against the other?
a: The bombs were not finished yet
38026.e: Each side could have struck back immediately. This was called the ‘balance of terror’.
38026.m: Fear of mutual destruction prevented a nuclear war.

38027.q: Where were schoolchildren in the USA supposed to duck during a nuclear alarm drill?
38027.e: In the ‘Duck and Cover’ drill, children learned to duck under their desk and protect their head.
38027.m: Schoolchildren in the USA practised ducking under their desks during an alarm.

38028.q: Roughly how many nuclear weapons did the USA and the Soviet Union have together in the 1980s?
38028.e: Around 1986 there were about 70,000 nuclear weapons in the world. Almost all of them belonged to the two superpowers.
38028.m: In the 1980s there were tens of thousands of nuclear weapons.

38029.q: What is meant by the ‘hotline’ in the Cold War?
a: A cable car across the border
38029.e: The hotline was a direct link between the governments of the two superpowers. It meant they could send each other messages quickly.
38029.m: The hotline was a direct communication line between the superpowers.

38030.q: Which two cities did the hotline connect?
38030.e: The line connected the government of the USA with the government of the Soviet Union. It ran through several European countries.
38030.m: The hotline connected Washington and Moscow.

38031.q: In which year was the hotline set up?
38031.e: The link went into operation on 30 August 1963. That was a few months after a dangerous crisis.
38031.m: The hotline was set up in 1963.

38032.q: After which dangerous event was the hotline set up?
a: After the fall of the Berlin Wall
38032.e: In the crisis over nuclear missiles in Cuba, it took a long time for messages to arrive. That was never to happen again.
38032.m: The hotline was a lesson learned from the Cuban Missile Crisis.

38033.e: The two superpowers wanted to prevent a nuclear war breaking out because of a mistake. With the direct line they could quickly clear up what was going on.
38033.m: The hotline was meant to prevent misunderstandings and an accidental war.

38034.q: Was the hotline really a telephone at the beginning?
38034.e: At first, written texts were sent over the line with a teleprinter. A teleprinter is a kind of typewriter that sends texts over a line.
38034.m: At first the hotline was a teleprinter, not a telephone.

38035.q: What is the hotline often popularly called?
38035.e: Many people and many films talk about the ‘red telephone’. Red stands for danger and importance.
38035.m: The hotline is often called the red telephone.

38036.q: Which animals were in the English sentence used to test the hotline?
38036.e: The first test sentence was ‘The quick brown fox jumped over the lazy dog’s back’. This sentence contains every letter of the English alphabet.
38036.m: The hotline was tested with a sentence about a fox and a dog.

38037.q: What are the peaceful protests in East Germany in 1989 called?
38037.e: Many people in East Germany took to the streets without violence and demanded freedom. In the end the government had to give in.
38037.m: The Peaceful Revolution of 1989 changed East Germany without violence.

38038.q: Which two superpowers faced each other in the Cold War?
a: The USA and the Soviet Union
38038.e: In the Cold War, the USA and the Soviet Union faced each other. They did not fight each other directly, but they built up huge amounts of weapons.
38038.m: In the Cold War, the USA and the Soviet Union faced each other.

38039.q: What did the USA and the Soviet Union agree on in 1987?
a: To get rid of certain nuclear missiles
To set up a joint army
38039.e: In the INF Treaty, both sides promised to destroy all their land-based intermediate-range missiles. That was an important step towards disarmament.
38039.m: In 1987 the superpowers agreed to get rid of certain nuclear missiles.

38040.q: Which US President was in office when the Berlin Wall fell in 1989?
38040.e: George Bush, the father of the later President George W. Bush, was President of the USA from 1989 to 1993.
38040.m: George Bush was President of the USA when the Wall fell.

38041.q: Who climbed onto a tank in Moscow in August 1991 and helped stop a coup?
38041.e: Opponents of the reforms wanted to seize power. From a tank, Boris Yeltsin called on people to resist, and the coup failed.
38041.m: In 1991 Boris Yeltsin stood on a tank against the coup.

38042.q: Which Soviet republic was the first to declare itself independent in 1990?
38042.e: On 11 March 1990 Lithuania declared its independence from the Soviet Union. Other republics followed afterwards.
38042.m: In 1990 Lithuania was the first Soviet republic to declare independence.

38043.q: What is the long human chain of 1989 through Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania called?
38043.e: On 23 August 1989, about two million people held hands. In this way they peacefully demanded freedom for their countries.
38043.m: In the Baltic Way, millions of people formed a human chain for freedom.

38044.q: Which country became the largest successor state of the Soviet Union in 1991?
38044.e: At the end of 1991 the Soviet Union broke up into 15 independent states. The largest of them is Russia, with its capital Moscow.
38044.m: Russia is the largest successor state of the Soviet Union.

38045.q: Which former Eastern Bloc country joined NATO in 1999?
38045.e: In March 1999 Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic became members of NATO. They had previously been in the Warsaw Pact.

38046.q: In which city stood the famous wall that divided a city from 1961 to 1989?
38046.e: The Berlin Wall divided the city of Berlin into an eastern and a western part. It stood for about 28 years.
38046.m: The Berlin Wall divided the city of Berlin.

38047.q: In its best-known form, what was the Berlin Wall mainly made of?
38047.e: In the end the Wall was built from large concrete sections. At the beginning it was partly just barbed wire and stones.
38047.m: In the end the Berlin Wall was made of concrete sections.

38048.q: Roughly how high was the Berlin Wall?
38048.e: The concrete wall was about 3.6 metres high. That is about twice as tall as an adult.
38048.m: The Berlin Wall was about 3.6 metres high.

38049.q: What was the guarded strip behind the Berlin Wall called, where people were killed trying to escape?
38049.e: Behind the Wall lay a wide, guarded strip with fences and watchtowers. Because people trying to escape were shot there, it was called the death strip.
38049.m: The strip behind the Wall was called the death strip.

38050.q: From where did border soldiers watch the Berlin Wall?
38050.e: There were many watchtowers along the Wall. From there, border soldiers made sure that no one escaped.
38050.m: Border soldiers guarded the Wall from watchtowers.

38051.q: Which state had the Berlin Wall built?
38051.e: The government of East Germany had the Wall built. The Soviet Union agreed to it.
38051.m: East Germany built the Berlin Wall.

38052.q: Roughly how long was the border around West Berlin?
38052.e: The Wall and the border installations around West Berlin were about 155 kilometres long. Part of it ran right through the middle of the city.
38052.m: The border around West Berlin was about 155 kilometres long.

38053.q: What did the East German government officially call the Berlin Wall?
38053.e: East Germany spoke of the ‘Anti-Fascist Protective Rampart’. In truth, the Wall was mainly meant to stop its own people from escaping.
38053.m: East Germany called the Wall a protective rampart.

38054.q: On which date did the building of the Berlin Wall begin?
38054.e: On Sunday, 13 August 1961, soldiers and police officers sealed off the border. After that, the Wall was built.
38054.m: The building of the Wall began on 13 August 1961.

38055.q: On the first day of building the Wall, what was mainly used to seal off the border?
38055.e: First, barbed wire and barriers were put up. Only in the days that followed was a solid wall built.
38055.m: At the beginning, the border was made of barbed wire.

38056.q: At what time of day did the sealing of the border begin on 13 August 1961?
38056.e: The sealing off began at night, when most people were asleep. In the morning the city was suddenly divided.
38056.m: The border was sealed off overnight.

38058.q: What happened to many families in Berlin after the Wall was built?
a: They were allowed to move to the West together
They all had to move to Bonn
They could visit each other freely every Sunday
38058.e: The Wall separated relatives and friends who lived on different sides. For a long time they could no longer visit each other.
38058.m: The Wall separated many families from each other.

38059.q: Which politician said in June 1961: ‘No one has the intention of building a wall’?
38059.e: Walter Ulbricht was the most powerful politician in East Germany at the time. Only two months after he said this, the building of the Wall began.
38059.m: Walter Ulbricht promised not to build a wall, and then did.

38060.q: What did the young border soldier Conrad Schumann do on 15 August 1961?
38060.e: Conrad Schumann jumped over the barbed wire to West Berlin. A photo of his jump became world-famous.
38060.m: Conrad Schumann escaped with a famous jump over the barbed wire.

38061.q: Which state did East Berlin belong to?
38061.e: East Berlin was the eastern part of Berlin. It belonged to the communist state in the east of Germany.
38061.m: East Berlin belonged to East Germany.

38062.q: Which tall tower with a silver ball was built in East Berlin?
38062.e: The Berlin TV Tower stands in what used to be East Berlin. It was finished in 1969 and is over 360 metres tall.
38062.m: The Berlin TV Tower comes from East Berlin.

38063.q: Which country was in charge of the east of Berlin after the Second World War?
38063.e: After the war, Berlin was divided into four parts. The eastern part was run by the Soviet Union.
38063.m: East Berlin used to be the Soviet part of the city.

38064.q: How can you recognise the little traffic-light man (Ampelmännchen) from East Berlin?
a: He has a dog with him
38064.e: The East Berlin traffic-light man has a hat on his head. Today he is very popular all over Berlin.
38064.m: The traffic-light man with a hat comes from East Germany.

38065.q: After the Wall was built, could people from East Berlin simply travel to West Berlin?
38065.e: After the Wall was built, most people from East Berlin were no longer allowed to go to the West. Only a few, for example pensioners, later got permission.
38065.m: People in East Berlin could not travel freely to the West.

38066.q: Which large square lies in the centre of former East Berlin?
38066.e: Alexanderplatz was an important square in East Berlin. A huge demonstration took place there on 4 November 1989.

38067.q: Which popular children’s character was on East German television every evening?
38067.e: The Sandman was on East German television from 1959. With a short story, he sent the children off to bed.
38067.m: The Sandman is a character from East German television.

38068.q: What was West Berlin often called because it lay in the middle of East Germany?
38068.e: West Berlin was completely surrounded by East Germany. That is why the city was often called an island.
38068.m: West Berlin was like an island in East Germany.

38069.q: Which three countries were in charge of West Berlin after the Second World War?
38069.e: After the war, Berlin was divided into four sectors. The three western sectors belonged to the USA, Great Britain and France.
38069.m: West Berlin was made up of three sectors of the Western powers.

38070.q: What did Berliners call the aeroplanes that supplied West Berlin in 1948 and 1949?
38070.e: During the blockade, planes brought food and coal to West Berlin. Because some pilots dropped sweets, they were called raisin bombers.
38070.m: The raisin bombers supplied West Berlin from the air.

38071.q: Which US President said ‘Ich bin ein Berliner’ (‘I am a Berliner’) in West Berlin in 1963?
38071.e: John F. Kennedy visited West Berlin in June 1963. With this sentence he showed that the USA stood by West Berlin.
38071.m: In 1963 John F. Kennedy showed his loyalty to West Berlin with a famous sentence.

38072.q: Which US President demanded in front of the Brandenburg Gate in 1987 that the Wall be torn down?
38072.e: Ronald Reagan called out: ‘Mr Gorbachev, tear down this wall!’ With this he challenged the Soviet leader to tear down the Wall.
38072.m: In 1987 Ronald Reagan demanded that the Wall be torn down.

38073.q: Which state was West Berlin closely linked to?
38073.e: West Berlin was closely linked to the Federal Republic of Germany. For example, it had the same currency, the Deutschmark.
38073.m: West Berlin was closely linked to West Germany.

38074.q: After the Wall was built, where were people from East Berlin usually allowed to travel?
a: Only to other Eastern Bloc countries
To every country in the world
38074.e: People from East Berlin were usually only allowed to travel to other Eastern Bloc countries such as Hungary or Czechoslovakia. People from West Berlin, on the other hand, could travel freely, including to Switzerland.
38074.m: West Berliners could travel much more freely than East Berliners.

38075.q: What does the abbreviation GDR stand for?
38075.e: GDR means German Democratic Republic (in German: DDR). That was the name of the state in the east of Germany from 1949 to 1990.
38075.m: GDR is short for German Democratic Republic.

38076.q: What was the capital of East Germany?
38076.e: East Germany made East Berlin its capital. The government and the party were based there.
38076.m: East Berlin was the capital of East Germany.

38077.q: Which tools could be seen in the emblem on the flag of East Germany?
38077.e: On East Germany’s black, red and gold flag there was an emblem with a hammer and a compass in a ring of ears of corn. That made it easy to recognise.
38077.m: The East German flag showed a hammer and compass.

38078.q: What was the name of the long-time leader of East Germany who had to resign in 1989?
38078.e: Erich Honecker led East Germany from 1971 to 1989. In October 1989 he had to resign after huge protests.
38078.m: Erich Honecker was the leader of East Germany for many years.

38079.q: In which part of Germany was the GDR?
38079.e: The GDR lay in the east of today’s Germany. That is why it was also called East Germany.
38079.m: The GDR lay in the east of Germany.

38080.q: Which sentence did people chant at the demonstrations in East Germany in 1989?
a: We are staying in the GDR
38080.e: At the Monday demonstrations, for example in Leipzig, thousands chanted ‘We are the people’. They wanted freedom and a say.
38080.m: ‘We are the people’ was the chant of the demonstrations in East Germany.

38081.q: What was the money in East Germany called?
38081.e: In East Germany people paid with the mark of the GDR. It was worth much less than the Deutschmark in the West.
38081.m: In East Germany people paid with the East German mark.

38082.q: What does the abbreviation FRG stand for?
38082.e: FRG means Federal Republic of Germany (in German: BRD). That was the name of the western German state, and it is still Germany’s name today.
38082.m: FRG is short for Federal Republic of Germany.

38083.q: Which city was the capital of West Germany before reunification?
38083.e: The small city of Bonn on the Rhine was the capital of West Germany. But it was only seen as a temporary capital.
38083.m: Bonn was the capital of the old West Germany.

38084.q: In which year was the Federal Republic of Germany founded?
38084.e: The Federal Republic was founded on 23 May 1949. On that day its Basic Law came into force.
38084.m: The Federal Republic of Germany was founded in 1949.

38085.q: What colours is the flag of the Federal Republic of Germany?
38085.e: The flag of the Federal Republic has black, red and gold stripes. It has no emblem in the middle.
38085.m: The German flag is black, red and gold.

38086.q: What was the money in West Germany called before the euro?
38086.e: In West Germany people paid with the Deutsche Mark, Deutschmark for short. Since 2002 people in Germany have paid with the euro.
38086.m: The Deutschmark was the money of West Germany.

38087.q: What is the head of government in the Federal Republic of Germany called?
38087.e: The Federal Chancellor leads the German government. In Switzerland, the Federal Council with seven members does this.
38087.m: In Germany, the Federal Chancellor leads the government.

38088.q: Which neighbouring country does the Federal Republic of Germany border to the south?
38088.e: Switzerland lies south of Germany. The border runs, for example, along the Rhine near Basel and Schaffhausen.
38088.m: Germany is a northern neighbour of Switzerland.

38089.q: Compared with East Germany, in which direction did the old West Germany lie?
38089.e: West Germany lay west of East Germany. That is why it was called West Germany.
38089.m: The FRG was the western part of Germany.

38090.e: Checkpoint Charlie was a well-known border crossing between East and West Berlin. It was in use from 1961 to 1990.
38090.m: Checkpoint Charlie was a border crossing in Berlin.

38091.q: On which street was the Checkpoint Charlie border crossing?
38091.e: Checkpoint Charlie was on Friedrichstrasse in Berlin. Today a small hut there reminds people of the border crossing.

38092.q: Which soldiers guarded Checkpoint Charlie on the Western side?
38092.e: Checkpoint Charlie was in the American sector of Berlin. That is why American soldiers were stationed there.
38092.m: American soldiers were stationed at Checkpoint Charlie.

38093.q: What faced each other at Checkpoint Charlie in October 1961?
38093.e: In October 1961, American and Soviet tanks faced each other. Luckily both sides drove away again after about 18 hours.
38093.m: In 1961, tanks faced each other at Checkpoint Charlie.

38094.q: What does the word ‘Charlie’ in the name Checkpoint Charlie stand for?
38094.e: In the phonetic alphabet, Charlie stands for the letter C. It was the third checkpoint, after Alpha and Bravo.
38094.m: In the phonetic alphabet, Charlie means the letter C.

38095.q: Who was mainly allowed to use Checkpoint Charlie?
38095.e: At Checkpoint Charlie it was mainly foreigners, diplomats and Allied soldiers who were allowed to cross the border. There were other crossings for West Germans.
38095.m: Checkpoint Charlie was mainly a crossing for foreigners.

38096.q: What did the famous sign at Checkpoint Charlie say?
a: You are leaving the American sector
38096.e: The sign warned: ‘You are leaving the American sector’. The sentence was written on it in English, Russian, French and German.
38096.m: The sign at Checkpoint Charlie warned that you were leaving the American sector.

38097.q: What reminds people of the past at Checkpoint Charlie today?
38097.e: At the former border crossing there is now a copy of the checkpoint hut with sandbags. Many tourists take photos there.
38097.m: Today there is a replica checkpoint hut at Checkpoint Charlie.

38098.q: What stands on top of the Brandenburg Gate?
38098.e: On top of the gate stands the Quadriga. It is a goddess on a chariot pulled by four horses.
38098.m: On the Brandenburg Gate stands the Quadriga with four horses.

38099.q: In which city is the Brandenburg Gate?
38099.e: The Brandenburg Gate stands in the middle of Berlin. It is one of Germany’s best-known landmarks.
38099.m: The Brandenburg Gate is a landmark of Berlin.

38100.q: Which French emperor took the Quadriga to Paris in 1806?
38100.e: Napoleon conquered Berlin in 1806 and had the figures taken to Paris. In 1814 they came back to Berlin.
38100.m: Napoleon took the Quadriga to Paris in 1806.

38101.q: At the time of the Wall, could you walk through the Brandenburg Gate?
38101.e: The Brandenburg Gate was right next to the Wall in the restricted zone. No one was allowed to simply walk through.
38101.m: At the time of the Wall, the Brandenburg Gate was closed off.

38102.q: When was the Brandenburg Gate opened to pedestrians again after the fall of the Wall?
38102.e: On 22 December 1989 a passage was opened at the Brandenburg Gate. Thousands of people celebrated.
38102.m: The Brandenburg Gate was opened shortly before Christmas 1989.

38103.q: What is the Brandenburg Gate a symbol of today?
38103.e: It used to stand for division because it was right by the Wall. Today it is a symbol of German unity.
38103.m: The Brandenburg Gate is a symbol of a united Germany.

38104.q: How many passageways does the Brandenburg Gate have?
38104.e: Between the columns of the gate there are five passageways. The middle one used to be only for the king.
38104.m: The Brandenburg Gate has five passageways.

38105.q: Which century does the Brandenburg Gate date from?
38105.e: The gate was built from 1788 to 1791. That is in the 18th century, so much earlier than the Wall.
38105.m: The Brandenburg Gate is over 200 years old.

38107.q: What was the Trabant affectionately called?
38107.e: The Trabant was usually just called ‘Trabi’. The name is still well known today.
38107.m: The Trabant was popularly called the Trabi.

38108.q: What special material was the outer body of the Trabant made of?
38108.e: The outer body of the Trabant was made of a hard plastic called Duroplast. Underneath there was a steel frame.
38108.m: The Trabi had a plastic body.

38109.q: Roughly what was the top speed of a Trabi?
38109.e: The Trabant had a small two-stroke engine. It could only manage just over 100 kilometres per hour. It was built in Zwickau.
38109.m: A Trabi could go at most about 100 km/h.

38110.q: How long did people in East Germany often have to wait for a new Trabant?
38110.e: There were too few cars in East Germany. That is why people often had to wait many years for their Trabi.
38110.m: People often waited many years for a new Trabi.

38111.q: After the fall of the Wall, what did many people from East Germany drive to the West in?
38111.e: After the border opened, long queues of Trabis drove to the West. The rattling cars became a symbol of the fall of the Wall.
38111.m: The Trabi became a symbol of the fall of the Wall.

38112.q: How many doors did the normal Trabant saloon have?
38112.e: The Trabant saloon only had two doors. Anyone who wanted to sit in the back had to fold the front seat forwards.
38112.m: The Trabi saloon had two doors.

38113.q: Until which year was the Trabant built?
38113.e: The last Trabant was built in April 1991. Altogether about three million were made.

38114.q: On the night the Wall fell, what did many people climb onto at the Brandenburg Gate?
38114.e: In front of the Brandenburg Gate the Wall was wide and flat on top. Many people stood and danced there during the night.
38114.m: When the Wall fell, many people stood on top of the Wall.

38115.q: What did many people do on the night the Wall fell?
38115.e: People from East and West hugged, cheered and drank together. For many, it was the best night of their lives.
38115.m: On the night the Wall fell, people from East and West celebrated.

38116.q: Which East German politician announced the new travel rules on television on 9 November 1989?
38116.e: Günter Schabowski read out the new travel rules at a press conference. The press conference was shown on television.
38116.m: Günter Schabowski announced the opening of the border.

38117.q: Which word did Günter Schabowski say when asked from when the new travel rules applied?
38117.e: Schabowski said: ‘As far as I know, this takes effect immediately, without delay.’ After that, thousands streamed to the border crossings.
38117.m: Schabowski said the travel rules applied immediately.

38118.q: At what time of day were the first border crossings opened on 9 November 1989?
38118.e: The press conference was in the evening. Late in the evening, under pressure from the crowds, the border soldiers opened the first crossings.
38118.m: The border opened late in the evening of 9 November.

38119.q: What did visitors from East Germany receive in the West as a welcome?
38119.e: Every visitor from East Germany received 100 Deutschmarks of welcome money in the West. Many used it to buy bananas, chocolate or presents.
38119.m: Visitors from East Germany received welcome money in the West.

38120.q: What happened at the border crossings in Berlin on the night of 9 November 1989?
a: The border soldiers opened the gates
The border soldiers built new walls
38120.e: Thousands of people pushed towards the border crossings. Under this pressure, the border soldiers opened the gates late in the evening.
38120.m: On the night the Wall fell, the border crossings opened.

38121.q: What were the people who chipped pieces off the Wall after it fell called in Berlin?
38121.e: These people hacked at the Wall like a woodpecker hacks at wood. That is why they were called ‘Mauerspechte’, wall woodpeckers.
38121.m: Wall woodpeckers chipped pieces off the Berlin Wall.

38122.q: Which tools did the wall woodpeckers usually work with?
38122.e: The wall woodpeckers knocked small pieces out of the concrete with a hammer and chisel. This made holes in the Wall.
38122.m: Wall woodpeckers used a hammer and chisel.

38123.q: What could be heard at many places along the Wall in the days after it fell?
38123.e: Everywhere wall woodpeckers were knocking pieces out of the concrete. That is why there was constant knocking and hammering at the Wall.
38123.m: After the Wall fell, knocking and hammering could be heard all along it.

38124.q: What did many wall woodpeckers do with the pieces they chipped off?
a: They threw them into the river
38124.e: Many people kept the colourful pieces of the Wall as a memento. Some also sold them to tourists.
38124.m: Pieces of the Wall became popular souvenirs.

38125.q: Why were many pieces of the Wall colourful on one side?
a: They were painted in the West
They had been in the rain
38125.e: On the West Berlin side the Wall was covered in graffiti. That is why many pieces were colourful on one side.
38125.m: The western side of the Wall was brightly painted.

38126.q: When were the wall woodpeckers mainly out and about?
a: After the fall of the Wall
38126.e: The wall woodpeckers came in the weeks and months after 9 November 1989. Now they no longer had to be afraid of border soldiers.
38126.m: Wall woodpeckers only appeared after the Wall fell.

38127.q: Where can you find real pieces of the Wall from wall woodpeckers today?
a: In many countries around the world
38127.e: Pieces of the Wall were taken all over the world and given away. You can find them in museums and homes in many countries.
38127.m: Pieces of the Berlin Wall can be found all over the world today.

38128.q: On which day was Germany reunified?
38128.e: On 3 October 1990 East Germany joined the Federal Republic. Since then there has been a single Germany again.
38128.m: Germany has been reunified since 3 October 1990.

38129.q: What is the German public holiday on 3 October called?
38129.e: On 3 October Germany celebrates reunification. The holiday is called the Day of German Unity.
38129.m: 3 October is the Day of German Unity.

38130.q: Which two states were united into one Germany in 1990?
38130.e: East Germany and West Germany were united in 1990. That is how today’s Germany came about.
38130.m: In 1990 West and East Germany became one country.

38131.q: Who was the German Chancellor at the time of reunification?
38131.e: Helmut Kohl was Federal Chancellor from 1982 to 1998. He is seen as the ‘Chancellor of Unity’.
38131.m: Helmut Kohl was the Chancellor of reunification.

38132.q: Which city became the capital of Germany after reunification?
38132.e: Since reunification, Berlin has been the capital of Germany. The government and parliament later moved from Bonn to Berlin.
38132.m: Berlin is the capital of united Germany.

38133.q: How many federal states has Germany had since reunification?
38133.e: Today Germany has 16 federal states. By comparison, Switzerland has 26 cantons.

38134.q: Which money did people in East Germany already get in the summer of 1990?
38134.e: On 1 July 1990 the Deutschmark was introduced in East Germany. That was an important step before reunification.
38134.m: East Germany got the Deutschmark in the summer of 1990.

38135.q: How many new federal states came from former East Germany?
38135.e: From East Germany came Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia. On top of that, East Berlin was united with West Berlin.
38135.m: Former East Germany brought five new federal states.

38136.q: What is the longest still standing section of the Berlin Wall called?
38136.e: The East Side Gallery is the longest surviving section of the Wall. It is in the district of Friedrichshain.
38136.m: The East Side Gallery is the longest section of the Wall still standing.

38137.q: What can you see on the East Side Gallery?
38137.e: In 1990 more than a hundred artists from 21 countries painted the Wall. This created an open-air gallery.
38137.m: The East Side Gallery is a wall full of artworks.

38138.q: On which river is the East Side Gallery?
38138.e: The East Side Gallery stands on the bank of the Spree in Berlin. The Spree flows right through the middle of the city.
38138.m: The East Side Gallery is on the Spree.

38139.q: Roughly how long is the East Side Gallery?
38139.e: The East Side Gallery is about 1316 metres long. That is about 1.3 kilometres.
38139.m: The East Side Gallery is just over a kilometre long.

38140.q: Which famous picture on the East Side Gallery shows two politicians kissing?
38140.e: The painting by Dmitri Vrubel shows the kiss between Leonid Brezhnev and Erich Honecker. It is called the Fraternal Kiss.
38140.m: The Fraternal Kiss is the best-known picture on the East Side Gallery.

38141.q: What does the ‘Window of Remembrance’ at the Berlin Wall Memorial show?
a: Photos of people who died at the Wall
The coats of arms of all countries
38141.e: The memorial is on Bernauer Strasse in Berlin. In the Window of Remembrance, photos remember the people who lost their lives trying to get across the Wall.
38141.m: The Window of Remembrance remembers the victims of the Wall.

38142.q: How can you tell in Berlin today where the Wall used to stand?
38142.e: In many streets, a double row of cobblestones shows where the Wall ran. This means you can follow it.
38142.m: Cobblestones in the ground show where the Wall stood.

38143.q: What does the Berlin Wall Memorial especially remember?
38143.e: The memorial remembers the people who died at the Wall. For many of them there is a photo in the ‘Window of Remembrance’.
38143.m: The memorial remembers the victims of the Wall.

38144.q: What can you see from the viewing platform at the Berlin Wall Memorial?
38144.e: From the platform you look out over a preserved section of the border installations. This shows you how wide the border strip was.
38144.m: At the memorial you can see a preserved border strip.

38145.q: What do many people in China use to eat instead of a fork?
38145.e: In China people have eaten with two thin sticks for a very long time. They use them to pick up rice, vegetables and meat.
38145.m: In China people often eat with chopsticks.

38146.q: How many yellow stars are on the flag of China?
38146.e: The Chinese flag shows one big and four small yellow stars. Together that makes five stars.
38146.m: Five yellow stars shine on the flag of China.

38147.q: Which very long structure is in China?
38147.e: The Great Wall of China is a huge old defensive wall. It stretches for thousands of kilometres across northern China.
38147.m: The Great Wall of China is one of the longest structures in the world.

38148.q: Which black and white animal lives in the wild only in China?
38148.e: The giant panda lives in the wild only in mountain forests in China. It mainly eats bamboo.
38148.m: The giant panda lives in the wild only in China.

38149.q: What is the money in China called?
38149.e: In China people pay with the yuan. The yen is the money of Japan.
38149.m: In China people pay with yuan.

38150.q: Which country has had more inhabitants than China since 2023?
38150.e: For a long time China was the country with the most people. According to the UN, India has had slightly more inhabitants since about 2023.
38150.m: India now has slightly more inhabitants than China.

38151.q: What is the huge square in the middle of Beijing called?
38151.e: In English, Tiananmen Square means ‘Square of the Gate of Heavenly Peace’. It is one of the largest squares in the world.
38151.m: Tiananmen Square is the big square in Beijing.

38153.e: Mao grew up in a village in Hunan province. His father was a farmer with his own land.
38153.m: Mao Zedong was the son of a farmer.

38154.q: Where does a huge picture of Mao hang?
a: On the Gate of Heavenly Peace in Beijing
On the Eiffel Tower in Paris
On the Federal Palace in Bern
38154.e: A large picture of Mao hangs above the entrance to the old imperial city in Beijing. It is one of the best-known pictures in China.
38154.m: A large picture of Mao hangs on the Gate of Heavenly Peace.

38155.q: What is the famous retreat of Mao’s troops in 1934 and 1935 called?
38155.e: On the Long March, Mao’s troops moved across China for about a year. They were fleeing from their enemies and covered thousands of kilometres.
38155.m: The Long March made Mao famous in China.

38156.q: What is the small book of Mao’s sayings called?
38156.e: The book had a red cover and was small. In the past, many people in China had to learn from it.
38156.m: Mao’s sayings are in the Little Red Book.

38157.q: In which year did Mao Zedong die?
38157.e: Mao died in Beijing in September 1976. He was 82 years old.

38158.q: By which title was Mao usually addressed?
38158.e: Mao was Chairman of the Communist Party. That is why people often said ‘Chairman Mao’.

38159.q: Where does Mao’s body lie today?
38159.e: Mao’s body lies in a large building, a mausoleum. Visitors can walk past it there.
38159.m: Mao lies in a mausoleum in Beijing.

38160.q: What is the troubled period in China that began under Mao in 1966 called?
38160.e: In the Cultural Revolution, many people were persecuted and old things were destroyed. It lasted about ten years.
38160.m: The Cultural Revolution was a hard time for China.

38161.q: In which sea is the island of Cuba?
38161.e: Cuba is the largest island in the Caribbean. It is warm there all year round.
38161.m: Cuba is a large island in the Caribbean.

38162.q: What is the capital of Cuba?
38162.e: Havana is the capital and largest city of Cuba. It lies on the north coast of the island.
38162.m: The capital of Cuba is Havana.

38163.q: Which large country is only about 150 kilometres from Cuba?
38163.e: Between Cuba and the US state of Florida there is only a narrow stretch of sea. The shortest distance is about 150 kilometres.
38163.m: Cuba is very close to the USA.

38164.q: Which language is spoken in Cuba?
38164.e: Cuba was a Spanish colony for a long time. That is why the people there speak Spanish.

38165.q: What are the streets of Havana known for?
a: For lots of old American cars
For lots of new electric cars
38165.e: Many cars from the 1950s are still driven in Cuba. New cars are rare and expensive there.
38165.m: Lots of old, colourful cars drive around Havana.

38166.q: Which plant is sugar made from in Cuba?
38166.e: Sugar cane is a tall grass that grows in warm countries. For a long time Cuba was one of the biggest sugar producers in the world.
38166.m: In Cuba, sugar is made from sugar cane.

38167.e: The cha-cha-cha was invented in Cuba around 1950. Cuba is known for its cheerful music and dances.
38167.m: The cha-cha-cha is a dance from Cuba.

38168.q: Which country is the only communist-ruled country in the Americas?
38168.e: In Cuba the Communist Party governs as the only party allowed. The other countries in the Americas have elections with several parties.
38168.m: Cuba is the only communist country in the Americas.

38169.q: What had Fidel Castro studied at university?
38169.e: Castro studied law in Havana and became a lawyer. After that he went into politics.
38169.m: Fidel Castro was a trained lawyer.

38170.q: How could you recognise Fidel Castro in many pictures?
a: By his beard and green uniform
By his top hat and tailcoat
By his bald head and suit
38170.e: Castro almost always had a full beard. He usually appeared in an olive-green uniform as well.
38170.m: Fidel Castro wore a beard and a green uniform.

38171.q: Who became President of Cuba after Fidel Castro in 2008?
38171.e: Fidel Castro was ill and gave up the office. His younger brother Raúl Castro took over.
38171.m: After Fidel Castro, his brother Raúl ruled Cuba.

38172.q: In which year did Fidel Castro die?
38172.e: Fidel Castro died in Havana in November 2016. He was 90 years old.

38173.q: Which famous comrade-in-arms of Fidel Castro came from Argentina?
38173.e: Ernesto ‘Che’ Guevara was a doctor and came from Argentina. He fought at Fidel Castro’s side.
38173.m: Che Guevara was a comrade-in-arms of Fidel Castro.

38174.q: Roughly how long did Fidel Castro rule Cuba?
38174.e: Castro ruled from 1959 to 2008. That is 49 years, almost half a century.
38174.m: Fidel Castro ruled Cuba for almost 50 years.

38175.q: What were Fidel Castro’s speeches known for?
38175.e: Castro gave very long speeches. At the UN in 1960, for example, he spoke for more than four hours.
38175.m: Fidel Castro often gave speeches lasting hours.

38176.q: In which mountain range in Cuba did Castro and his fighters hide?
38176.e: The Sierra Maestra is a mountain range in south-eastern Cuba. From there, Castro’s people fought against the government.
38176.m: Castro’s fighters hid in the Sierra Maestra.

38177.q: What is the capital of Vietnam?
38177.e: Hanoi lies in the north of Vietnam. Since reunification it has been the capital of the whole country.
38177.m: The capital of Vietnam is Hanoi.

38178.q: Which leader is the former city of Saigon named after today?
38178.e: Ho Chi Minh was the founder of communist Vietnam. Since 1976 Saigon has been called Ho Chi Minh City.
38178.m: Vietnam’s largest city bears the name of Ho Chi Minh.

38179.q: Which large country fought against North Vietnam in the Vietnam War?
38179.e: The USA supported South Vietnam with many soldiers. They fought against communist North Vietnam.
38179.m: In the Vietnam War, the USA fought against North Vietnam.

38180.q: In which year did the Vietnam War end?
38180.e: In April 1975 troops from the North captured the city of Saigon. That was the end of the war.

38181.q: What does Vietnam look like on the map?
a: Long and narrow like an S
Triangular like a slice of cake
38181.e: Vietnam stretches a long way along the coast. Its shape is like the letter S.
38181.m: Vietnam is long and narrow like an S.

38182.q: Which grain is grown most in Vietnam?
38182.e: In Vietnam there are many rice fields that stand under water. Rice is the most important food there.
38182.m: A lot of rice is grown in Vietnam.

38183.q: Which hat do many people in Vietnam wear when working in the fields?
a: A pointed conical hat made of leaves
A woolly hat with a bobble
38183.e: The conical hat is woven from palm leaves. It protects against sun and rain.
38183.m: In Vietnam, a pointed conical hat protects against sun and rain.

38184.q: What is the well-known noodle soup from Vietnam called?
38184.e: Pho is a soup with rice noodles, herbs and often beef. Ramen, on the other hand, comes from Japan.
38184.m: Pho is a noodle soup from Vietnam.

38185.q: What is the famous bay with lots of rocky islands in Vietnam called?
38185.e: In Ha Long Bay almost 2000 limestone rocks rise out of the sea. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
38185.m: Ha Long Bay in Vietnam has countless rocky islands.

38186.q: What is the capital of North Korea?
38186.e: Pyongyang is the capital and largest city of North Korea. Seoul is the capital of South Korea.
38186.m: The capital of North Korea is Pyongyang.

38187.q: Which country does North Korea border to the south?
38187.e: The Korean peninsula is divided into two countries. North Korea is in the north, South Korea in the south.
38187.m: South Korea lies south of North Korea.

38188.q: Who was the first ruler of North Korea?
38188.e: Kim Il-sung led North Korea from 1948 until his death in 1994. Since then his descendants have ruled.
38188.m: Kim Il-sung was the first ruler of North Korea.

38189.q: Who is the ruler of North Korea (as of 2026)?
38189.e: Kim Jong-un has led North Korea since the end of 2011. He is the grandson of the first ruler.
38189.m: North Korea is ruled by Kim Jong-un.

38190.q: In which country did North Korea’s current ruler go to school as a teenager?
38190.e: In the 1990s he went to schools near Bern. At the time he used a different name.
38190.m: North Korea’s ruler went to school in Switzerland as a teenager.

38191.q: Which war took place from 1950 to 1953?
38191.e: In the Korean War, the north of the peninsula fought against the south. Korea has been divided ever since.
38191.m: The Korean War lasted from 1950 to 1953.

38192.q: Which neutral country has had officers on the border between North and South Korea since 1953?
38192.e: Swiss officers monitor the ceasefire there together with Sweden. It is one of Switzerland’s oldest peace missions.
38192.m: Since 1953 Switzerland has helped to monitor the peace in Korea.

38193.q: What can be seen in the middle of the flag of North Korea?
38193.e: The flag is blue, red and white. There is a red star in a white circle.
38193.m: There is a red star on North Korea’s flag.

38194.q: What is the capital of Laos?
38194.e: Vientiane lies on the river on the border with Thailand. It is the capital of Laos.
38194.m: The capital of Laos is Vientiane.

38195.q: What does the country of Laos not have?
38195.e: Laos is surrounded by other countries on all sides. Like Switzerland, it has no coastline.
38195.m: Like Switzerland, Laos has no access to the sea.

38196.q: Which big river flows through Laos?
38196.e: The Mekong is one of the longest rivers in Asia. It is very important for Laos, for example for fishing.
38196.m: The Mekong is the most important river in Laos.

38197.q: Which religion do most people in Laos follow?
38197.e: Most people in Laos are Buddhists. All over the country there are many temples and monks in orange robes.
38197.m: Most people in Laos are Buddhists.

38198.q: Since which year have the communists ruled Laos?
38198.e: In December 1975 the king was removed from power. Since then a communist party has ruled Laos alone.
38198.m: The communists have ruled Laos since 1975.

38199.q: What is a highland area in Laos world-famous for?
a: Hundreds of ancient, huge stone jars
38199.e: On the so-called Plain of Jars there are hundreds of huge stone jars that are very old. What they were used for is not fully known.
38199.m: In Laos there are many old stone jars on a plain.

38200.q: Which country is a neighbour of Laos?
38200.e: Laos borders Thailand, Vietnam, China, Cambodia and Myanmar. Japan, India and Indonesia are not neighbours.
38200.m: Thailand is a neighbour of Laos.

38201.q: Which buildings shape the old royal city of Luang Prabang in Laos?
38201.e: Luang Prabang used to be the royal city of Laos. Because of its many temples it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
38201.m: Luang Prabang is a city of temples in Laos.

38202.q: Which large country in Central Asia became independent after the end of the Soviet Union?
38202.e: Kazakhstan was one of the republics of the Soviet Union. In December 1991 it became a state of its own.
38202.m: Kazakhstan has been independent since the end of the Soviet Union.

38203.q: Into how many countries did the Soviet Union break up?
38203.e: The Soviet Union was made up of 15 republics. Each of them became a country of its own.

38204.q: How is the Soviet Union abbreviated in English?
38204.e: USSR stands for ‘Union of Soviet Socialist Republics’. That was the full name of the Soviet Union.
38204.m: The Soviet Union is abbreviated to USSR.

38205.q: What was the long conflict between East and West that stopped with the end of the Soviet Union called?
38205.e: In the Cold War, the USA and the Soviet Union were hostile to each other. But they did not fight each other directly with weapons.
38205.m: The Cold War ended with the end of the Soviet Union.

38207.q: Which union of states was founded by former Soviet republics in December 1991?
38207.e: CIS stands for ‘Commonwealth of Independent States’. Many former parts of the Soviet Union worked together in it.
38207.m: The CIS was formed in 1991 from former Soviet republics.

38208.q: Which three small countries on the Baltic Sea regained their independence in 1991?
38208.e: Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania are called the Baltic states. They belonged to the Soviet Union until 1991.
38208.m: Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania are the Baltic states.

38209.q: Which large country with the capital Kyiv became independent in 1991?
38209.e: Ukraine declared its independence in August 1991. Before that it belonged to the Soviet Union.
38209.m: Ukraine has been an independent country since 1991.

38210.q: Where did Mikhail Gorbachev grow up?
38210.e: Gorbachev grew up in the countryside in the south of Russia. Even as a teenager he helped with the grain harvest.
38210.m: Gorbachev grew up in a village in the countryside.

38211.q: In which year did Gorbachev come to power?
38211.e: In March 1985 Gorbachev became head of the Communist Party. That made him the most powerful man in the Soviet Union.

38212.q: Which prize did Gorbachev receive in 1990?
38212.e: Gorbachev helped to end the conflict between East and West peacefully. For this he received the Nobel Peace Prize.
38212.m: Gorbachev received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1990.

38213.q: What was particularly noticeable on Gorbachev’s face?
a: A large birthmark on his forehead
38213.e: Gorbachev had a large reddish birthmark on his head. You could recognise him by it at once.
38213.m: Gorbachev had a striking birthmark on his forehead.

38214.q: What does the Russian word ‘glasnost’ mean?
38214.e: With glasnost, Gorbachev wanted problems to be talked about more openly. Newspapers were allowed to report more.

38215.q: In which Swiss city did Gorbachev meet US President Ronald Reagan in 1985?
38215.e: In November 1985 the two politicians met for the first time in Geneva. The meeting helped to reduce tensions between East and West.
38215.m: Gorbachev and Reagan met in Geneva in 1985.

38216.q: In which year did Mikhail Gorbachev die?
38216.e: Gorbachev died in Moscow in August 2022. He was 91 years old.

38217.q: Which country is the largest country in the world?
38217.e: Russia is almost twice as big as Canada, the second-largest country. It lies in both Europe and Asia.
38217.m: Russia is the largest country in the world.

38218.q: Who became the first President of Russia in 1991?
38218.e: Boris Yeltsin was elected President in June 1991. He stayed in office until the end of 1999.
38218.m: Boris Yeltsin was the first President of Russia.

38219.q: Which script is Russian written in?
38219.e: Russian is written with Cyrillic letters. Some of them look like ours but sound different.
38219.m: Russian is written with Cyrillic letters.

38220.q: What is the long railway line from Moscow to the Pacific called?
38220.e: The Trans-Siberian Railway is over 9000 kilometres long. The whole journey by train takes about a week.
38220.m: The Trans-Siberian Railway is one of the longest railway lines in the world.

38221.q: Which city is the second-largest city in Russia?
38221.e: St Petersburg lies on the Baltic Sea. It used to be the capital of the Russian tsars.
38221.m: St Petersburg is the second-largest city in Russia.

38222.q: Which lake in Russia is the deepest lake in the world?
38222.e: Lake Baikal in Siberia is over 1600 metres deep. No other lake in the world is as deep.
38222.m: Lake Baikal is the deepest lake in the world.

38223.q: What are the Russian wooden dolls that fit inside each other called?
38223.e: A matryoshka can be opened. Inside is a smaller doll, inside that an even smaller one, and so on.
38223.m: The matryoshka is a Russian doll with many dolls inside.

38224.q: What is the Kremlin in Moscow?
a: A fortress with palaces and churches
38224.e: The Kremlin is surrounded by a high wall with towers. Inside there are palaces, churches and government buildings.
38224.m: The Kremlin is a fortress in the middle of Moscow.

38225.q: Who has his official seat in the Kremlin today?
38225.e: The Russian President works in the Kremlin. That is why people often say ‘the Kremlin’ when they mean the Russian government.
38225.m: The Russian President works in the Kremlin.

38226.q: What colour is the Kremlin wall?
38226.e: The Kremlin wall is built of red bricks. It is over two kilometres long.

38227.q: What shines on five of the Kremlin’s towers?
38227.e: Large stars made of red glass sit on five towers. At night they are lit from inside.
38227.m: Red stars shine on five Kremlin towers.

38228.q: What is the Kremlin tower with the big clock called?
38228.e: The Spasskaya Tower has a large tower clock with chimes. Its bells ring in the New Year in Russia.
38228.m: The Spasskaya Tower is the Kremlin’s clock tower.

38229.q: Which huge bell stands in the Kremlin?
38229.e: The Tsar Bell is the largest bell in the world. A piece broke off, so it has never been rung.
38229.m: The Tsar Bell, the largest bell in the world, stands in the Kremlin.

38230.q: On which river is the Kremlin?
38230.e: The Moskva flows right through the middle of Moscow. The city also gets its name from it.
38230.m: The Kremlin is on the Moskva.

38231.q: What does the Russian word ‘kremlin’ mean?
38231.e: A kremlin is a fortified castle in a Russian city. Other old cities in Russia have a kremlin too.
38231.m: The word kremlin means castle or fortress.

38232.q: In which city is Red Square?
38232.e: Red Square is in the middle of Moscow, right next to the Kremlin. It is the best-known square in Russia.

38233.q: What is the colourful church on Red Square called?
38233.e: St Basil’s Cathedral was built almost 500 years ago. With its colourful towers it is a landmark of Moscow.
38233.m: St Basil’s Cathedral is the colourful church on Red Square.

38234.q: What shape are the colourful domes of St Basil’s Cathedral?
38234.e: The domes are round at the bottom and pointed at the top. That is why they are called onion domes.
38234.m: St Basil’s Cathedral has colourful onion domes.

38235.q: Whose body lies in a mausoleum on Red Square?
38235.e: Lenin founded the first communist state. After his death in 1924 his body was put on display in a mausoleum.
38235.m: Lenin lies in a mausoleum on Red Square.

38236.q: In old Russian, what did the word ‘red’ mean in the name ‘Red Square’?
38236.e: The Russian word ‘krasnaya’ used to mean ‘beautiful’ as well. So the name originally meant ‘beautiful square’.
38236.m: Red Square originally meant something like beautiful square.

38237.q: Which big celebration with soldiers usually takes place on Red Square on 9 May?
38237.e: On 9 May Russia remembers the end of the Second World War in Europe. Soldiers and tanks then parade across the square.
38237.m: The Victory Parade takes place on Red Square on 9 May.

38238.q: Which big old department store stands on Red Square?
38238.e: GUM is a long department store with glass roofs. It was built over 100 years ago.
38238.m: The GUM department store stands on Red Square.

38239.q: What have Red Square and the Kremlin been part of since 1990?
a: The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World
38239.e: In 1990 UNESCO declared Red Square and the Kremlin World Heritage. This is meant to protect them for ever.
38239.m: Red Square is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

38240.q: What should parliament pay attention to when electing the Federal Council?
a: That regions and language areas are represented
That everyone is the same age
That everyone has the same job
38240.e: According to the Federal Constitution, the various regions and language areas should be fairly represented on the Federal Council.
38240.m: The regions and language areas should be represented on the Federal Council.

38241.q: What happens if nobody reaches an absolute majority in a Federal Council election?
a: There is another round of voting
The President of the Confederation chooses someone
The election is postponed for a year
38241.e: Voting continues until someone has more than half the votes. Whoever has the fewest votes drops out at a later stage.
38241.m: In a Federal Council election, voting continues until someone has an absolute majority.

38242.q: Who may choose first when the departments are allocated?
38242.e: The seniority principle applies: whoever has been on the Federal Council longest chooses first. Newly elected members often get the department that is left over.
38242.m: When departments are allocated, the longest-serving Federal Councillor goes first.

38243.q: What does the German abbreviation EFD stand for?
38243.e: The EFD (in English FDF) looks after federal finances, taxes and customs. Every year it draws up the Confederation's budget.
38243.m: The EFD is the Confederation's finance department.

38244.q: What is the department called that the President of the Confederation heads during the presidential year?
38244.e: In the presidential year, the President of the Confederation keeps their own department. It is then called the presidential department and is supported by a presidential service.
38244.m: The President of the Confederation's department is called the presidential department.

38245.q: Who has headed the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs (FDFA) since November 2017 (as of 2026)?
38245.e: Ignazio Cassis from Ticino was elected to the Federal Council in 2017 and took over the FDFA on 1 November 2017.
38245.m: Ignazio Cassis has headed the foreign affairs department since 2017.

38246.q: What is the head of the FDFA (Federal Department of Foreign Affairs) usually called in everyday language?
38246.e: The FDFA looks after relations with other countries. That is why its head is often called the foreign minister.
38246.m: The person who leads the FDFA is often called the foreign minister.

38247.q: Which directorate of the FDFA deals with development cooperation and humanitarian aid?
38247.e: SDC stands for Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation. It supports projects in poorer countries and provides humanitarian aid, for example after disasters.
38247.m: The SDC is Switzerland's development agency within the FDFA.

38248.q: Which directorate of the FDFA helps Swiss people who get into trouble abroad?
a: The Office of the Attorney General
38248.e: The Consular Directorate looks after Swiss people living abroad and travellers. For example, it offers a helpline and travel advice.
38248.m: In an emergency abroad, the FDFA's Consular Directorate helps.

38249.q: What do you call an official mission of Switzerland in the capital city of another country?
38249.e: An embassy represents Switzerland to the government of another country. It is led by an ambassador and belongs to the FDFA.
38249.m: An embassy represents Switzerland in another country.

38250.q: Which directorate of the FDFA is responsible for questions of international law?
38250.e: The Directorate of International Law advises the federal government on questions of international law, for example on treaties or international humanitarian law.
38250.m: The FDFA has its own directorate for international law.

38251.q: What does the abbreviation DDPS stand for?
38251.e: The DDPS is the Federal Department of Defence, Civil Protection and Sport. Among other things, the Swiss Armed Forces belong to it.
38251.m: The DDPS covers defence, civil protection and sport.

38252.q: Which important organisation belongs to the DDPS?
38252.e: The Swiss Armed Forces belong to the Department of Defence, Civil Protection and Sport. It also looks after civil protection and sport.
38252.m: The army belongs to the DDPS.

38253.q: Who has led the DDPS since 1 April 2025 (as of 2026)?
38253.e: Martin Pfister from the canton of Zug was elected to the Federal Council on 12 March 2025. He took over the DDPS on 1 April 2025.
38253.m: Martin Pfister has led the DDPS since 2025.

38254.q: Who was the first woman to head the defence department?
38254.e: Viola Amherd from Valais took over the DDPS in 2019. Before that, the department had always been led by men.
38254.m: Viola Amherd was Switzerland's first female defence minister.

38255.q: Which federal office in the DDPS is responsible for sport?
38255.e: FOSPO stands for Federal Office of Sport. Its headquarters are in Magglingen near Biel, and among other things it runs the programme “Youth and Sport”.
38255.m: The Federal Office of Sport belongs to the DDPS.

38256.q: Which federal office in the DDPS makes the official national maps of Switzerland?
38256.e: swisstopo is the Federal Office of Topography. It surveys Switzerland and publishes the national maps.
38256.m: Switzerland's national maps come from swisstopo.

38257.q: Which federal office in the DDPS is responsible for protecting the population in disasters?
38257.e: The Federal Office for Civil Protection (FOCP) coordinates protection in disasters and emergencies. The National Emergency Operations Centre also belongs to it.
38257.m: In disasters, the Federal Office for Civil Protection coordinates help.

38258.q: Which body in the DDPS buys weapons, vehicles and equipment for the army?
38258.e: armasuisse is the Federal Office for Defence Procurement. It buys and tests equipment for the army.
38258.m: armasuisse buys the equipment for the Swiss Armed Forces.

38259.q: Who has led DETEC since 2023 (as of 2026)?
38259.e: Albert Rösti from the canton of Bern was elected to the Federal Council in December 2022. He has led DETEC (Environment, Transport, Energy and Communications) since the start of 2023.
38259.m: Albert Rösti has headed DETEC since 2023.

38260.q: Which federal office in DETEC is responsible for railways and public transport?
38260.e: FOT stands for Federal Office of Transport. It supervises the trains, buses, boats and cable cars of public transport.
38260.m: The Federal Office of Transport is responsible for railways and public transport.

38261.q: Which federal office in DETEC supervises aviation in Switzerland?
38261.e: FOCA stands for Federal Office of Civil Aviation. For example, it is responsible for the safety of airports and airlines.
38261.m: Civil aviation is supervised by FOCA.

38262.q: Which federal office in DETEC looks after nature, forests, water and air?
38262.e: FOEN stands for Federal Office for the Environment. It is responsible for protecting natural resources and using them sustainably.
38262.m: The Federal Office for the Environment protects nature, forests, water and air.

38263.q: Which federal office in DETEC is responsible for radio, television and telecommunications?
38263.e: OFCOM stands for Federal Office of Communications. For example, it regulates mobile phone frequencies as well as radio and television.
38263.m: OFCOM is the Federal Office of Communications.

38264.q: Which federal office in DETEC is responsible for the national roads?
38264.e: FEDRO stands for Federal Roads Office. It builds and maintains Switzerland's motorways and national roads.
38264.m: The Federal Roads Office FEDRO is responsible for the motorways.

38265.q: Which federal office in DETEC deals with energy matters such as electricity and saving energy?
38265.e: SFOE stands for Swiss Federal Office of Energy. It works for a secure and sustainable energy supply.
38265.m: The Federal Office of Energy is responsible for the energy supply.

38266.q: Are the meetings of the Federal Council open to the public?
a: Yes, they are shown on television
38266.e: The discussions in the Federal Council are confidential. This lets the members talk openly with each other before they decide together.
38266.m: What the Federal Council discusses stays confidential.

38267.q: Roughly how many items of business does the Federal Council deal with each year?
38267.e: In its meetings, the Federal Council deals with around 2,500 items of business every year, including many motions from parliament.
38267.m: The Federal Council decides on thousands of items of business every year.

38270.q: What usually happens when a member of the Federal Council stands for election again?
38270.e: Sitting Federal Council members are almost always re-elected. That is why many stay in office for several terms.
38270.m: Sitting Federal Councillors are usually re-elected.

38271.q: How long does someone stay in office if they are elected to the Federal Council in a by-election?
a: Until the end of the current term
38271.e: The successor takes over the seat only for the rest of the term. After that, they must stand in the general election.
38271.m: In a by-election, the election only counts until the end of the term.

38272.q: What is it called when a party proposes two candidates to the Federal Assembly for a seat on the Federal Council?
38272.e: Parties often propose two people so that parliament has a choice. This is called a two-person ticket.
38272.m: With a two-person ticket, a party gives parliament a choice.

38273.q: Who was elected to the Federal Council in December 2022 as Ueli Maurer's successor?
38273.e: Albert Rösti was elected in the first round on 7 December 2022. He beat Hans-Ueli Vogt, who was also on the SVP ticket.
38273.m: Albert Rösti succeeded Ueli Maurer in 2022.

38274.q: Who succeeded Federal Councillor Didier Burkhalter after he stepped down in 2017?
38274.e: Ignazio Cassis was elected on 20 September 2017. For the first time since 1999, someone from Italian-speaking Switzerland sat on the Federal Council again.
38274.m: Ignazio Cassis became Didier Burkhalter's successor in 2017.

38275.q: Can parliament remove a member of the Federal Council during their term of office?
a: Yes, if the President of the Confederation wants it
38275.e: A Federal Council member stays in office until the end of the four-year term, unless they resign or die. Only at the general election can they fail to be re-elected.
38275.m: A Federal Councillor cannot be voted out during their term.

38276.q: Who elects the Vice-President of the Federal Council?
38276.e: The President and Vice-President of the Federal Council are elected every year by the Federal Assembly from among the Federal Councillors.
38276.m: The Federal Assembly elects the Vice-President of the Federal Council.

38277.q: For how long is the Vice-President of the Federal Council elected?
38277.e: Like the presidency, the vice-presidency lasts one calendar year. Then there is a new election.
38277.m: The Vice-President of the Federal Council is in office for one year.

38278.q: In which year was Elisabeth Kopp elected to the Federal Council?
38278.e: The election took place on 2 October 1984, 13 years after women got the right to vote at federal level.
38278.m: Elisabeth Kopp became a Federal Councillor in 1984.

38279.q: Which department did Elisabeth Kopp lead?
38279.e: From 1984 to 1989, Elisabeth Kopp led the Federal Department of Justice and Police (FDJP).

38280.q: What is Elisabeth Kopp known for in Swiss history?
a: She was the first woman on the Federal Council
She was the first female federal judge
She was the first female pilot
38280.e: In 1984, Elisabeth Kopp was the first woman elected to the Federal Council. Before that, it had only had men.
38280.m: Elisabeth Kopp was the first woman on the Federal Council.

38281.q: Why did Elisabeth Kopp have to resign in 1989?
a: Because of a phone call with her husband
Because she lost a popular vote
Because of a dispute about her department
38281.e: She had phoned her husband to warn him to leave the board of a company that was suspected of money laundering. This “telephone affair” led to her immediate resignation in January 1989.
38281.m: The telephone affair ended Elisabeth Kopp's time in office.

38283.q: How did the criminal case against Elisabeth Kopp at the Federal Supreme Court end in 1990?
a: With a fine of one million francs
38283.e: In February 1990, the Federal Supreme Court acquitted her of breaching official secrecy, because it could not be proved that she had acted on purpose.
38283.m: Elisabeth Kopp was acquitted by the Federal Supreme Court.

38284.q: What was Ruth Dreifuss the first woman to be in 1999?
a: President of the Federal Supreme Court
38284.e: The Federal Assembly elected Ruth Dreifuss President of the Confederation for 1999. She was the first woman in this office.
38284.m: In 1999, Ruth Dreifuss was the first female President of the Confederation.

38285.q: Which party does Ruth Dreifuss belong to?
38285.e: Ruth Dreifuss is a Social Democrat. Before her election, she was central secretary of the Swiss Trade Union Federation.
38285.m: Ruth Dreifuss is a member of the SP.

38286.q: What was Ruth Dreifuss responsible for as a Federal Councillor, among other things?
38286.e: From 1993 to 2002, she led the Department of Home Affairs. There she was responsible for health and social insurance such as the AHV (old-age insurance), among other things.
38286.m: Ruth Dreifuss led the Department of Home Affairs.

38287.q: Which woman in order on the Federal Council was Ruth Dreifuss?
38287.e: The first female Federal Councillor was Elisabeth Kopp from 1984. Ruth Dreifuss was elected to the Federal Council in 1993 as the second woman.
38287.m: Ruth Dreifuss was Switzerland's second female Federal Councillor.

38288.q: What was Ruth Dreifuss before she was elected to the Federal Council?
38288.e: Ruth Dreifuss was central secretary of the Swiss Trade Union Federation. She was not a member of the federal parliament before her election.
38288.m: Ruth Dreifuss came to the Federal Council from the trade union movement.

38289.q: Which important law came into force in 1996 while Ruth Dreifuss was in office?
38289.e: The Health Insurance Act (KVG) came into force on 1 January 1996. Since then, basic health insurance has been compulsory for everyone.
38289.m: Compulsory health insurance was introduced under Ruth Dreifuss.

38290.q: Apart from her presidential year, what else was special about Ruth Dreifuss?
a: She was the first Jewish member of the Federal Council
She was the youngest female Federal Councillor ever
She had been President of the Council of States
She led two departments at the same time
38290.e: Ruth Dreifuss was the first member of the Federal Council of Jewish origin. She also had not sat in the federal parliament before her election.
38290.m: Ruth Dreifuss was the first Jewish member of the Federal Council.

38291.q: How often is a new official Federal Council photo published?
38291.e: Since 1993, there has been a new official Federal Council photo every year. It is published at the start of the year.
38291.m: There is a new Federal Council photo every year.

38292.q: Who usually stands in the middle of the official Federal Council photo or stands out in some other way?
a: The youngest member of the Federal Council
The newest member of the Federal Council
38292.e: On the Federal Council photo, the president is at the centre. The vice-president usually stands next to them, a little in the background.
38292.m: On the Federal Council photo, the President of the Confederation is the centre of attention.

38293.q: Who usually decides how the Federal Council photo of a year looks?
38293.e: The President of the Confederation chooses the theme of the photo and works on it with a photographer.
38293.m: The President of the Confederation chooses the theme of the Federal Council photo.

38294.q: How are the other members usually arranged on the Federal Council photo?
a: By how long they have been in office
